638.title: Grace after meals
638.hook: four blessings: for food, for the land, for Jerusalem, for goodness
638.howItsDone: After a meal with bread, observant Jews recite Birkat HaMazon, usually from a small booklet called a bencher; on Shabbat and holidays it is often sung together at the table, with extra passages for the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' five words for Miriam. Your line was both are real prayer. Who got your five-word wish? Today, a prayer that isn't short at all, and comes at the moment most people are reaching for their coats. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

In a lot of homes, grace comes first. The food is hot, everyone's hungry, someone says a few words, and the forks come out. Jewish tradition does have a blessing before the meal: the short one over bread, thanking God who brings forth bread from the earth. But the big one, the one the Torah actually commands, comes after. When the plates are empty and you're full and a little sleepy and nobody needs anything. That's exactly the moment the Torah picks.
screen: `GRACE BEFORE THE FORKS.` → `A SHORT BLESSING OVER BREAD.` → `THE BIG ONE COMES AFTER.`

segments.voice: The source is in Deuteronomy: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." Eat, be satisfied, bless. In that order. The rabbis read this as the command for Birkat HaMazon, the blessing for food. Its core is four blessings, and the Talmud, in Berakhot 48b, tells a story about where each came from. The first, for food, thanks God who feeds the whole world. The tradition says Moses composed it when the manna began to fall in the desert. The second, for the land, thanks God for the good land, and for the covenant and the Torah. Tradition credits Joshua, when the people entered the land. The third asks for mercy on Jerusalem and its rebuilding; it's linked to David and Solomon, who made the city a capital and built the Temple. The fourth is later, and its story is sad. After the Romans crushed the revolt at Betar, the dead lay unburied for a long time. When permission to bury them finally came, the sages at Yavneh added a blessing: to the One who is good and does good. Good, that the bodies had not decayed. Good, that they could finally be buried. A blessing for goodness, born in grief. Together they trace a whole history, from the desert to the land to the city to the ruins and back to gratitude. Many Jews sing it, especially on Shabbat, and it can take several minutes. A full stomach turns into a short history lesson in thanks.
screen: `EAT, BE SATISFIED, BLESS.` · `FOOD AND LAND: MOSES, JOSHUA.` · `JERUSALEM: DAVID AND SOLOMON.` · `GOODNESS: BORN AFTER BETAR.` · then, large: `FOUR THANKS AFTER EATING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grace after one meal. Think back to the last thing you ate, or wait until your next meal is done. Then walk the four blessings in your own way. First, the food itself, and whoever grew it and cooked it. Second, the ground it came from. Third, a place you love and want to see whole. Fourth, one good thing in your life, even if it came out of something hard. If you pray, you can say the thanks to God. The bell holds the time.
Birkat HaMazon. The blessing for food: four blessings, for food, the land, Jerusalem and goodness, said when you're already full.
Your line: four thanks after eating. Today, after one meal, before you stand up, name four things to be thankful for: food, land, place, goodness. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

639.title: Three at the table
639.hook: when three eat together, one invites the others to bless
639.howItsDone: When three or more Jewish adults eat bread together, one leads the zimmun, the invitation to grace, and the others respond before Birkat HaMazon; with ten, the word Eloheinu is added. Who may lead and join varies between communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Birkat HaMazon, grace after meals. Your line was four thanks after eating. Did a meal end with food, land, place and goodness? Today, what changes when you're not eating alone. Day six hundred thirty-nine.

Friday night. The meal is over. Plates pushed back, someone's still picking at the cake. And then one person at the table clears their throat and says, half singing, in Yiddish or Hebrew: friends, let's bless. Everyone stops. They answer. It's a tiny call and response, maybe fifteen seconds long. And it only happens when there are at least three people who ate together. Two people bless on their own. Three become something else.
screen: `THE PLATES PUSHED BACK.` → `FRIENDS, LET'S BLESS.` → `ONLY WHEN THERE ARE THREE.`

segments.voice: It's called zimmun, an invitation, from a root that means to call together. The Mishnah in Berakhot rules that three who ate together are obligated to make it. The Talmud finds the source in a psalm: "O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt His name together." With me, together: one person invites, the others join. Here's how it goes in many homes. The leader says: friends, let us bless, in Hebrew rabbotai nevarech, or in the old Yiddish, rabbosai, mir vellen bentshen. Everyone answers with a verse from Psalm 113: "Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and for ever." The leader repeats it, then says: let us bless the One whose food we have eaten. And the table answers: blessed is the One whose food we have eaten, and through whose goodness we live. Then the grace continues. With ten people, God's name, Eloheinu, our God, is added to the invitation. The Talmud also says that women may form a zimmun of their own. In some communities today men and women together, or women leading, are welcomed; in others, practice stays more traditional. Communities differ, and each follows its own teachers. What's striking is the shape. Not one person thanking alone. Someone has to ask the others to join, and they have to say yes out loud. A meal shared becomes thanks shared. The table turns into a small congregation for a minute.
screen: `ZIMMUN: CALLED TOGETHER.` · `MAGNIFY THE LORD WITH ME.` · `FRIENDS, LET US BLESS.` · `TEN ADD: OUR GOD.` · then, large: `LET US BLESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank together. Think of the next meal you'll share with at least two other people. Picture the moment it ends. Imagine being the one who says: before we get up, let's say thank you. Imagine them answering. If you pray, you can picture the zimmun itself, or the psalm's let us exalt His name together. If not, rehearse a simple invitation: let's thank whoever made this. Then sit with who's at that table. The bell holds the time.
Zimmun. The invitation. When three or more eat together, one calls the others to bless, and they answer before the grace.
Your line: let us bless. Today, after a shared meal, be the one who invites everyone to say thank you together. Day six hundred thirty-nine.

640.title: Any language (Mishnah Sotah 7:1)
640.hook: the Shema, Amidah and grace may be said in any language one understands
640.tomorrow: Siddur close: prayer shapes the day
640.howItsDone: Many Jewish communities pray mainly in Hebrew, with translations printed beside the text; Reform and some other communities include substantial prayer in the local language, and many individuals add personal prayers in their mother tongue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the zimmun: three at the table, and one invites the rest. Your line was let us bless. Did you get to be the one who asked? Today, the question of which language the blessing has to be in. Day six hundred forty.

Saturday morning, three synagogues, three cities. Hebrew in each of them. But listen closer. In one, the rabbi reads a prayer in English. In another, an old man murmurs a translation in Russian under his breath. In a third, the children sing a line in Spanish. Some people assume Jewish prayer only counts in Hebrew. The Mishnah took up that question directly, long before anyone printed a translated prayer book, and its answer was a list.
screen: `HEBREW IN EACH OF THEM.` → `ENGLISH, RUSSIAN, SPANISH.` → `DOES IT COUNT?`

segments.voice: The Mishnah, in tractate Sotah, gives a list of things that may be said in any language. Among them: the Shema, the tefillah, which means the Amidah, and Birkat HaMazon, the grace after meals we met two days ago. The three pillars of daily prayer. Any language. The Talmud explains the Shema in a lovely way. Shema means hear. Some sages read it as: hear in any language that you hear, that you understand. If the words don't reach you, what have you heard? Grace after meals is a blessing, and you can't really thank someone in words you don't follow. The Amidah is a plea for mercy, and you plead in whatever words you have. Not everything is in that list. The Mishnah has a second list of things that must be said in Hebrew, like the priestly blessing. And Hebrew holds a special place. It's the language of the Torah and of the prayer book, shared by Jews far apart. Many authorities in Jewish law say it's best to pray in Hebrew if you understand it, and some say Hebrew should be used even if you don't. Reform prayer books include a great deal of the vernacular; Orthodox prayer books keep the Hebrew and print translations beside it. Communities weigh it differently. But the Mishnah's baseline stands: the Shema, the Amidah and grace are valid in a language you understand. In the Mishnah's view, prayer doesn't wait for the right accent.
screen: `THE SHEMA, THE AMIDAH, THE GRACE.` · `SHEMA: HEAR, IN WHAT YOU HEAR.` · `SOME THINGS STAY IN HEBREW.` · `COMMUNITIES WEIGH IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `ANY LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray in your first language. Whatever language you dreamed in as a child, the one your grandmother scolded you in, use it now. If you pray, say a short prayer or blessing in it, slowly, and notice whether it lands differently. If you don't pray, say something you're grateful for in that language, out loud, and notice the same. If English is your only language, try saying it in the plainest English you can, the way you'd say it to a child. The bell holds the time.
Any language. The Mishnah's ruling that the Shema, the Amidah and the grace after meals may be said in any language you understand.
Your line: God understands every language. Today, say one thank-you in the language closest to your heart, even if it's just one word. Day six hundred forty.

641.title: Siddur close: prayer shapes the day
641.hook: morning, afternoon, evening, Shabbat, festivals: the prayer book is a map of time
641.tomorrow: Elul: the king in the field
641.howItsDone: Observant Jews pray three services daily, Shacharit, Mincha and Maariv, with added prayers for Shabbat, the new moon and festivals, all laid out in the siddur; many others keep one or two prayers, like Modeh Ani or the Shema at bedtime.

segments.voice: Yesterday, any language: the Shema, the Amidah and the grace, valid in words you understand. Your line was God understands every language. Which language did your thank-you come out in? Today, we close the prayer book. Day six hundred forty-one.

Back on day five hundred thirty-eight, we opened a book. A siddur. The word means order. For a hundred and four days we've walked it, roughly in the order it's prayed. Through the morning blessings and the rooster. The warm-up psalms. The Shema with a hand over the eyes. The Amidah on your feet. Kaddish, Aleinu, the afternoon pause, the evening's shelter. Shabbat welcomed like a bride. The festivals, the Days of Awe, and this last week, the prayers that live outside the book.
screen: `A BOOK CALLED ORDER.` → `A HUNDRED AND FOUR DAYS.` → `FROM THE ROOSTER TO THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Step back and look at the whole siddur, and you notice it isn't really organized by topic. It's organized by time. It's a map of the clock and the calendar. Morning, afternoon, evening: three services a day. The Talmud links them to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And the book of Genesis gives Isaac a beautiful moment for the afternoon: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." A psalm names all three times in a row: "Evening, and morning, and at noonday, will I complain, and moan; and He hath heard my voice." Then the week: six weekdays with their requests, and Shabbat, when the requests go quiet and the Amidah becomes one long breath of holiness. Then the month, with the new moon. Then the year: the festivals with Hallel, the Days of Awe with their own thick book. Then a life: a prayer for a journey, a blessing after food, the Kaddish after a death. Open the siddur anywhere and the first question it answers is: what time is it? That's the deep idea. Prayer in this tradition isn't mainly something you do when you feel like it. It's a rhythm laid over time, so that the day itself has a shape. The day wakes into thanks. It pauses in the middle. It lies down into shelter. The prayers come back around, again and again, until the day is held by them, the way a riverbank holds the river. Tomorrow we turn from the book to the year itself, beginning with Elul.
screen: `ORGANIZED BY TIME, NOT TOPIC.` · `MORNING, AFTERNOON, EVENING.` · `THE WEEK, THE MONTH, THE YEAR.` · `WHAT TIME IS IT?` · then, large: `PRAYER SHAPES THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one prayer to keep. Look back over the whole walk: the morning blessings, the rooster's understanding, the Shema, the Amidah's open my lips, Birkat HaMazon, the evening's spread over us, the traveler's prayer, five words for someone sick. Which one stayed with you? Pick one. Decide when in your day it will live: morning, midday, meal, night. If you pray, say it now, once, slowly. If not, say the line you chose as a line to live by. The bell holds the time.
Siddur. Order: the prayer book's name, read today as a map of time, day, week, month, year and a life.
Your line: prayer shapes the day. Today, put your one chosen prayer at its time, and let it mark that hour. Day six hundred forty-one.

642.title: Elul: the king in the field
642.hook: Shneur Zalman's parable: in Elul the king walks out to meet people in the fields
642.carry: the king is in the field
642.howItsDone: During Elul many Jews take stock of the past year, add Psalm 27 to daily prayer, give more charity and prepare for Rosh Hashanah; in Chabad and other Hasidic communities Shneur Zalman's parable of the king in the field is often retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday, we closed the siddur, the prayer book. Your line was prayer shapes the day. Which prayer did you choose to keep? Today, a new stretch of the path: the Jewish year in depth, starting with the month before the new year. Day six hundred forty-two.

To see a king in the old world, you had to earn it. You traveled to the capital. You waited outside the palace. Guards checked who you were. Officials decided whether you mattered enough. If you got in at all, you bowed, said your piece fast, and were walked out. Now suppose that once a year, the king leaves the palace. He rides out of the city into the countryside, and anyone working in the fields can walk right up to him.
screen: `TO SEE A KING, YOU EARNED IT.` → `GUARDS, OFFICIALS, WAITING.` → `ONCE A YEAR, HE RIDES OUT.`

segments.voice: This parable comes from Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, the founder of Chabad Hasidism. He told it about Elul, the last month of the Jewish year, the month just before Rosh Hashanah. Before a king enters his city, he says, the people go out to meet him in the field. There, anyone may approach him. He receives them all with a pleasant face, a shining countenance. Farmers in their work clothes. No appointment. Then he enters the city, and the people follow him to the palace, where only invited guests get in. The palace is Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: the grand, awesome days, the full congregation, the long services. The field is Elul. The quiet month before, when the closeness is easy and anyone can come as they are. There's an old way of finding Elul in a verse, too. The Song of Songs says: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine." In Hebrew, ani l'dodi v'dodi li. The first letters of those four words, aleph, lamed, vav, lamed, spell Elul. So the month itself is read as a love song between God and the people. During Elul many communities add Psalm 27 to their daily prayers, a psalm about seeking God's face and hoping to dwell in God's house. The point of the parable is a surprise. The month before judgment could be a month of dread. Shneur Zalman makes it a month of closeness. The king is out in the field, and the field is where you already are.
screen: `SHNEUR ZALMAN OF LIADI.` · `ANYONE MAY APPROACH IN THE FIELD.` · `THE PALACE IS THE DAYS OF AWE.` · `ANI L'DODI V'DODI LI: ELUL.` · then, large: `THE KING IS IN THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go out to meet something. If you can, step outside, or at least to a window. Look at what's actually there: the street, a tree, the sky, a parked car. Don't dress it up. This is the field. If you pray, you can picture the king of the parable out here, in the ordinary, receiving you as you are. If not, let yourself meet the day without preparing for it first. Just walk up to it. The bell holds the time.
Elul. The last month of the Jewish year, before Rosh Hashanah. The month, Shneur Zalman taught, when the king is in the field.
Your line: the king is in the field. Today, notice one moment when something good comes to meet you where you already are. Day six hundred forty-two.

643.title: Elul: getting ready
643.hook: the shofar sounds on Elul mornings, and prayers for forgiveness begin
643.howItsDone: In Ashkenazi synagogues the shofar is blown after weekday morning prayers during Elul, and selichot begin the Saturday night before Rosh Hashanah; Sephardi communities recite selichot early each morning throughout Elul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shneur Zalman's parable. Your line was the king is in the field. What came to meet you where you were? Today, how the field gets noisy. Day six hundred forty-three.

A weekday morning in late summer. The service is ending, people are folding their prayer shawls, someone is already checking their phone. And then, from the front, a sound that cuts through everything: a ram's horn. A long, raw blast, then broken notes, then a long one again. It isn't a holiday. Nobody's celebrating. It's just an ordinary Tuesday in Elul. In many synagogues, this happens every weekday morning for a month.
screen: `A WEEKDAY, LATE SUMMER.` → `A RAM'S HORN CUTS THROUGH.` → `EVERY MORNING FOR A MONTH.`

segments.voice: In Ashkenazi communities, the shofar is blown after the morning service through most of Elul, though not on Shabbat and not on the day before Rosh Hashanah. It's a wake-up call, a month early. The great medieval teacher Maimonides wrote that the shofar seems to say: sleepers, wake up from your sleep; look at your deeds and return. Then come the selichot, the prayers for forgiveness. Selichah means pardon. Sephardi communities rise early and say them through the whole month of Elul. Ashkenazi communities begin later, usually on the Saturday night before Rosh Hashanah, sometimes around midnight, and continue until Yom Kippur. Either way, the heart of every selichot service is the same: the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy. They come from the moment after the golden calf, when God passes before Moses and proclaims: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 17b, pictures God wrapping in a prayer shawl like a prayer leader and showing Moses this order of prayer, promising that whenever Israel recites it, they will be answered. So the selichot repeat it again and again. Why a whole month? Tradition says that Moses went back up the mountain for a second set of tablets at the start of Elul, and came down forty days later, on what became Yom Kippur. Elul is the runway. You don't arrive at the Days of Awe cold.
screen: `THE SHOFAR, EVERY WEEKDAY MORNING.` · `SLEEPERS, WAKE UP.` · `SELICHOT: PRAYERS FOR PARDON.` · `THE THIRTEEN ATTRIBUTES.` · then, large: `THIRTY DAYS TO GET READY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear a shofar, or a bell. If you can, find a recording of a shofar and play it now. If not, the bell at the start of this sit will do. Let the sound be a wake-up call. When it fades, ask yourself one honest question: what from this past year needs looking at? Don't solve it. Just let the question stand. If you pray, you can say the line from Exodus: merciful and gracious. The bell holds the time.
Selichot. Prayers for pardon, built around the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, said in the weeks before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Your line: thirty days to get ready. Today, write down one thing from this year you'd like to make right before the new one starts. Day six hundred forty-three.

644.title: Rosh Hashanah: the world's birthday
644.hook: the new year marks the sixth day of creation, when people were made
644.howItsDone: Rosh Hashanah is observed on the first two days of Tishrei with long synagogue services, the shofar, festive meals with apples and honey and round challah, and the words 'today the world was born' after the shofar in Musaf.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shofar on Elul mornings and the selichot. Your line was thirty days to get ready. What did you write down to make right? Today, the runway ends, and the new year begins. Day six hundred forty-four.

Most new year's celebrations are about a calendar turning over. A countdown, a ball dropping, a kiss at midnight. The Jewish new year is different, and you can hear it in the prayers. Right after the shofar is blown in the additional service, the congregation says a line in Hebrew: hayom harat olam. Today the world was conceived. Or born. Today. Not a calendar flipping. A birthday. And it isn't the Jewish people's birthday. It's everyone's.

Rosh Hashanah means head of the year. Interestingly, the Torah never uses that name for it. The Torah calls it the first day of the seventh month, "a memorial proclaimed with the blast of horns, a holy convocation." The rabbis gave it its famous name. In the Talmud, two great sages argue about when the world was created. Rabbi Eliezer says in the month of Tishrei, in the autumn. Rabbi Yehoshua says Nisan, in the spring. The prayer book follows Rabbi Eliezer for this day: the new year is the world's anniversary. A midrash makes it even more precise. If creation began on the twenty-fifth of Elul, then the first of Tishrei, Rosh Hashanah, is the sixth day. The day human beings were made. The midrash then tells the whole first day of Adam's life, hour by hour: created, given the breath of life, placed in the garden, given a command, broke it, judged, and pardoned, all before sunset. And God says to him: this is a sign for your children. As you stood before Me in judgment today and went out pardoned, so will they, every year on this day. So Rosh Hashanah holds two things at once. It's the day of judgment, solemn and serious. And it's a birthday party for the whole human race. Judgment, in this telling, is something that happens to beloved creatures, on the day they were made.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish the world a happy birthday. Sit, and picture the whole earth. Not an idea of it: the actual oceans, a city at night, a field, a crowded train, a baby somewhere being born right now. Every one of those people shares this birthday. If you pray, you can thank God for making the world, and for making people. If not, simply say it, quietly or out loud: happy birthday, world. Let it be as silly and as serious as it is. The bell holds the time.
Rosh Hashanah. Head of the year. The Jewish new year, remembered as the birthday of the world and the day people were made.
